correctness.rationale: The split has covariance zero and is jointly Gaussian, hence its selection and inference components are independent with the displayed variances. With \(\tau=\tan\theta\), the log discovery probability is \(g(\mu\cos\theta)+g(\mu\sin\theta-z)\), where \(g=\log\Phi\) has strictly negative second derivative because the inverse Mills ratio is strictly decreasing. Both inner sine/cosine terms have negative second derivative, so the objective is strictly concave. Endpoint derivative signs give one critical point; evaluating at \(\theta=\pi/4\) places it strictly to the inference-heavy side. The first-order equation gives the weak-signal limit uniformly. Independent numerical replay reproduced \(\tau_*(1,0.05)=2.322477560969451\) and the weak-signal limit \(2.585227122870808\), while the analytic proof supplies the quantifiers.

originality.rationale: The modern primary paper gives exactly the independent Gaussian \((U,V)\) decomposition, explains that the randomization variance allocates information between selection and inference, and explicitly says its information-averaging representation offers a possible way of selecting that variance. The inspected full text does not state the audited scalar sign-screen/independent-confirmation objective, its unique inverse-Mills optimizer, the strict \(\tau_*>1\) theorem, or the weak-signal closed form. Cox’s 1975 abstract is materially close because it studies split proportions in a normal-means significance problem, but the full article was not lawfully available in this run; under the owner rule that inaccessible plausible literature alone does not fail originality, it is retained as a specific residual risk rather than treated as proof of coverage.
residual_risks: Cox (1975) could contain a mathematically equivalent allocation calculation under its many-normal-means ordinary-splitting formulation; only its abstract was materially available in this run.
Older normal-theory screening/confirmation literature may use different terminology for the same scalar optimization; targeted searches did not locate it.

value.rationale: Information allocation is an explicit open design issue in the modern fission source. The audited theorem supplies a unique exact optimizer, proves a qualitative inference-heavy direction for every positive signal and conventional one-sided level, and yields a closed weak-signal benchmark while preserving the boundary-null probability. That is a motivated quantitative design law rather than an arbitrary numerical optimization.
residual_risks: The model is scalar, known-variance, one-sided, and optimizes joint screening-and-rejection probability rather than conditional selective power.

final_claim: For the independent Gaussian fission split \(U=X+\tau Z\), \(V=X-Z/\tau\) with one-sided sign screening and independent level-\(\alpha\) confirmation, the joint discovery probability has a unique maximizer \(\tau_*(\mu,\alpha)>1\), characterized by the displayed inverse-Mills equation; as \(\mu\downarrow0\), \(\tau_*\to e^{-z_{1-\alpha}^2/2}/(2\alpha)\), while at \(\mu=0\) the joint probability is exactly \(\alpha/2\) for every allocation.
scientific_limitations: Known-variance scalar Gaussian model with one-sided sign screening and independent confirmation only.
Cox (1975) remains a specifically identified access-limited originality risk.
